In summary, our research is concerned with

the question of why the London Congestion Charging scheme succeeded in 2003, but the similar proposals in Sheffield and Durham had previously failed, and how the London scheme was able to leave a legacy that enabled it to influence later events, in the form the successful introduction of the Western Extension in 2007.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the London congestion charge was the product of an unusual set of conditions, and that the charge itself was a relatively small part of a larger narrative that was itself a product of an even wider narrative.
the London congestion charge was a policy idea that was carried forward in a policy window, and that this policy window was created by the construction of a narrative.

the congestion charge was the result of a combination of factors, but that the most important of these was the narrative that was constructed to justify the policy, and the timing of the narrative’s appearance in relation to the policy window.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the London Congestion Charging Scheme (LCCS) was a success, and that it is now an accepted part of London life, but the LCCS was not the only policy idea in town.

we found that the policy window for the Congestion Charge was opened by the narrative that the Mayor of London was a ‘man in a hurry’, and that he had to act decisively to deliver his manifesto pledges.
narratives are a key mechanism by which policy ideas are carried forward in a policy window, and that they are also an important factor in the closure of windows.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the construction of narratives is a key factor in explaining why ideas rise and fall over time.
policy windows are not just a matter of timing, they are also a matter of meaning.
